extracted.intended_audience: students, writers, critics, and general readers interested in literary and rhetorical techniques (humour, satire, poetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Recognize, analyze, or produce bathos — the literary/rhetorical device where high/lofty style meets trivial or ludicrous subject matter — including its intentional uses in satire and accidental occurrences as artistic failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of bathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a lofty, elegant, or elevated style to present silly, vulgar, or trivial subject-matter, or a sudden transition from the former to the latter, thereby creating a ludicrous or comedic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs either accidentally (through artistic ineptitude) or intentionally as a rhetorical device (usually for the sake of comedy). Examples: Pope's Peri Bathous; modern usages across literature and the arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional vs accidental bathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish when bathos is a conscious rhetorical device for comedy (intentional) versus when it is an unconscious failure producing an unintended ludicrous effect (accidental).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentional bathos appears in satirical genres such as burlesque and mock epic; accidental bathos arises from ineptitude (e.g., a filmmaker intending fright who produces laughter). Assessment should note authorial intent and whether the juxtaposition is controlled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violation of decorum / radical juxtaposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The radical juxtaposition of the serious with the frivolous which violates decorum (the fittingness of the subject) and thereby creates humour with an unexpected and improper juxtaposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pope highlights combining very serious matters with very trivial ones as the most memorable method of 'sinking'. When evaluating use of bathos, look for breaches of genre-appropriate tone and surprising contrasts between register and subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bathos as failed attempt at sublimity (artistic ineptitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally referred to an amusingly failed attempt at presenting artistic greatness—a work meant to be sublime that instead 'sinks' into the ludicrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to judge whether an instance is a sign of poor craft (e.g., overwrought or clumsy attempts at grandeur) rather than deliberate satire. Pope's Peri Bathous lists many methods for writing poorly; many evaluations hinge on whether the 'sinking' seems deliberate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use in satirical genres and mock-heroic techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Bathos is used intentionally in satirical genres such as burlesque and mock epic and in mock-heroic works to undercut the sublime for comedic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should note genre conventions (e.g., Rape of the Lock) and whether the device functions as targeted satire of lofty pretensions rather than mere clumsiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic employment of tropes and figures of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Bathos often exploits tropes and figures of speech (undercutting, parody, ironic listing) to produce comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pope explains comic uses of tropes and figures; examples include juxtaposing a lover's death with a lapdog's death or listing grievous losses that trivialize the sublime. Evaluate the selection and subversion of rhetorical figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to pathos (distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bathos should not be confused with pathos: pathos is the successful arousal of sympathy and pity, whereas bathos produces the ludicrous or comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging emotional effect, distinguish whether the work moves the audience to genuine sympathy (pathos) or to ridicule/laughter (bathos). Mislabeling can lead to incorrect critical assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surreal humour and the absurd when mixing serious with trivial intentionally
rubrics_metrics.description: When artists consciously mix the very serious with the very trivial, the effect can be surreal humour and the absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate intentional mixtures by their produced atmosphere (surreal/absurd) and whether the audience perceives deliberate play between registers. Contrast with unconscious bathos, which feels unintentional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete-arts manifestations: kitsch and camp
rubrics_metrics.description: Kitsch (replication of serious or sublime subjects in a trivial context) can express bathos in the concrete arts; a tolerant/detached enjoyment of naïve/unconscious bathos is an element of camp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess visual/aesthetic works for trivializing high art (e.g., Last Supper prints on tea-towels) and for camp sensibility (Sontag's 'Notes on Camp') that accepts naive bathos as aesthetic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Film techniques that produce bathos: contrast cuts and jump cuts
rubrics_metrics.description: In film, bathos may appear in a contrast cut intended for comic relief or be produced by an accidental jump cut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating cinematic bathos, identify editing choices that create abrupt register shifts. Determine whether cuts are staged for humor (contrast cut) or accidental/clumsy (jump cut) yielding unintended bathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pope's 'Art of Sinking' methods (practical markers of bad verse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pope's manual enumerates numerous methods for 'sinking' in poetry; of these, the combining of very serious matters with very trivial ones is the most remembered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Pope's examples (e.g., the academic hierarchy of genres, the 'stiffen' example about still life, mock-heroic undercutting) as concrete markers when diagnosing bathetic failures or deliberate mockery in verse and prose.
